title: Why Does Lust Feel Like Love?
paragraphs:
Why Does Lust Feel Like Love?
The Dangerous Counterfeit That Feels So Right Until It Breaks You—and the Savior Who Still Calls You Home
There are wounds that bleed where no one can see them.
There are addictions hidden behind smiles, worship songs, wedding rings, dating apps, late-night scrolling, private messages, secret tabs, and silent regrets.
There are people reading these words who genuinely love Jesus... yet feel trapped by desires they never wanted to have.
Some have already crossed lines they swore they never would.
Some have built entire lives around a relationship they secretly know God never designed.
And perhaps the most painful question they carry is not, "Why did I sin?"
Why did it feel so much like love?
That question has haunted humanity since the Garden of Eden.
Because Satan rarely tempts people with something that looks evil.
He offers something that looks beautiful... while quietly removing God from the picture.
That is exactly what lust does.
It borrows the language of love.
It even feels spiritual at times.
But beneath its beautiful disguise lies something entirely different.
Lust is one of the greatest counterfeits ever created.
It wears love's clothing while stealing love's heart.
Scripture never treats lust as merely a problem of hormones.
When Jesus spoke about adultery, He shocked everyone listening.

"But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart."
(Matthew 5:28, KJV)
The Greek text uses the verb ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō).
It means far more than noticing beauty.
It means to desire in order to possess... to covet... to consume... to satisfy oneself.
No wonder lust often feels like love.
Both can keep you awake all night.
But only one survives when sacrifice becomes expensive.
The Bible has an entirely different word for love.
The New Testament often uses ἀγάπη (agapē).
It reflects the very character of God.
Not merely that God possesses love.
That means every definition of love must begin with Him—not with our feelings.
Modern culture tells us that if something feels deeply emotional, it must be authentic.
The Bible tells a different story.
The Hebrew word for "deceitful" is עָקֹב (ʿāqōḇ).
Something capable of leading us away from truth while convincing us we are right.
This explains why someone can sincerely believe they are "following their heart" while slowly walking away from God.
That is why Proverbs reminds us:

"Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding."
(Proverbs 3:5)
Lust often begins where loneliness goes untreated.
Not every lonely person becomes lustful.
But many lustful patterns begin with an empty soul searching for comfort.
But lust is like drinking saltwater.
Jesus described a completely different source of satisfaction.

"Whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst."
(John 4:14)
Notice where He spoke those words.
A man who was not her husband.
Yet Jesus never reduced her to her past.
He exposed her thirst before addressing her behavior.
Because underneath sexual brokenness often lives spiritual thirst.
This is one of the greatest themes running through Scripture.
People rarely seek sinful pleasures because sin itself is satisfying.
They seek them because they are starving for something only God can provide.

C. S. Lewis famously observed that our problem is not that our desires are too strong, but too weak—we settle for lesser pleasures instead of the joy God offers. His insight echoes the biblical pattern: humanity exchanges the glory of God for substitutes (Romans 1), even though only God can truly satisfy the soul.
He does not need to destroy your desire.
He only needs to redirect it.
In Genesis, temptation began with a question.
That question still echoes through every generation.
Did God really say purity matters?
Did God really say marriage is sacred?
Did God really say holiness leads to joy?
Did God really say obedience is better than immediate pleasure?
Every temptation is ultimately a question about God's goodness.
If Satan can convince you that God is withholding something better...
He never manipulated people into loving Him.
He never used power for personal gratification.
That is why Paul commands believers:
The Greek imperative φεύγετε (pheugete) is urgent.
Do not assume you are stronger than temptation.
Joseph understood this long before Paul wrote those words.
When Potiphar's wife pursued him, Joseph did not stay to prove his self-control.
Sometimes holiness looks less like standing bravely...
Every good gift finds its proper place under God's design.
Fire in a fireplace warms a home.
Fire on the living-room floor destroys it.
Sex inside God's covenant reflects His wisdom.
Sex outside His covenant carries consequences Scripture never hides.
Yet if this article ended there...
Because Christianity is not ultimately a story about avoiding scandal.
It is the story of a Savior who walks straight into scandal to rescue sinners.
The woman caught in adultery deserved condemnation according to those holding stones.
Jesus did not deny her sin.
He simply revealed that every accuser also needed mercy.
Then He spoke words that still echo through history:

"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more."
(John 8:11)
Not because sin did not matter.
Because Jesus would carry its punishment Himself.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We are not saved because our desires became pure.
We are saved because Christ remained perfectly pure in our place.
At the cross, justice and mercy kissed.
There the deepest scandal in history became the greatest display of grace.
God answered with forgiveness offered through the crucified and risen Christ.
That is why no addiction is stronger than His mercy.
The empty tomb declares louder still.
Jesus does not merely forgive sinful people.
The Holy Spirit does not renovate the old heart.

"A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you."
(Ezekiel 36:26)
Only God can change desires from the inside.
Perhaps today you recognize yourself somewhere in these words.
Maybe you have mistaken obsession for affection.
Jesus is not waiting for you to become clean enough before coming to Him.
He invites you to come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Repentance is not merely turning away from lust.
It is turning toward Someone infinitely better.
Toward the One whose nail-scarred hands prove that real love always gives before it asks.
Toward the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to find the one.
Toward the Bridegroom who laid down His life for His Bride.
Toward the King who wore a crown of thorns so sinners could receive crowns of life.
If this message exposed something hidden, do not hide any longer.
Bring it into the light before the One who already knows—and still calls you by name.
Your testimony may become the encouragement another struggling believer desperately needs.
One faithful act of sharing may place biblical truth in front of someone who is quietly crying out for hope.
Because one encounter with Jesus can rewrite a lifetime of regret.
